chapter_theme: Neelakesi ends her debate with Kundalakesi by mocking the Jataka tales of the Buddha's gifts of body and life as useless, harmful or false; the king rules the tales fictions, Kundalakesi names her teacher Arkkachandran and is driven out of the city, and Neelakesi refuses every reward, asks the king to keep dharma, and leaves through the sky for Ujjain.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist woman debater who planted the rose-apple branch as a challenge
the king of Kampili who presides over the debate between Neelakesi and Kundalakesi
the people of Kampili who drive the defeated Kundalakesi out of the city
the Buddhist teacher at Ujjain whom Kundalakesi names as her master

212.reading: Neelakesi sums up against Kundalakesi's catalogue of the Buddha's gifts: the one who proves his compassion by these birth-tales, she says, gives those who recite them only one and the same notion, and the line about a flame being lit seems to refer to one of the tales.
212.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 (ஆதனாற் குறந்தாங்கெழுவான், வேதமில் சுடரேற்று ஒருதாம் என்றான்) do not divide with confidence; only line 3, சாதகம் இவற்றான் அருள் சாதிப்பான், is clear, and it states the position the following verses attack: that the Jataka gifts establish the Buddha's grace.

claims.claim: the Buddha's tales of former births establish his compassion

213.reading: Neelakesi says the fool who gives eyes and other organs is like one who does not see that an ox has no milk, since those who asked for them never said what lack the gift would meet.
213.nuance: The argument turns the Jataka's praise of the asker-satisfying gift into a question about need: a gift is judged by what it supplies, not by what it costs the giver. மருதின் வாழ் பகை in line 4 is obscure.

claims.claim: a gift that meets no stated need of the receiver is folly, not generosity

214.reading: Neelakesi asks whether half a body split off becomes one with another's body: thinking so is folly, for the flesh is eaten only by crows, and an eye given is the same, since a body once broken does not join another.
214.nuance: The objection is practical, not moral: flesh and eyes cannot be grafted, so the famous gifts could not have helped anyone. பரகாயம் (another's body) is a borrowed technical word.

claims.claim: a part cut from one body cannot become part of another, so a gift of flesh or an eye benefits no one

215.reading: Since the self is present in both halves of a body cut in two, Neelakesi argues, the one who takes the half is the giver's killer, and if no awareness remains, cutting off a corpse and saying 'take it' is no gift at all.
215.nuance: The premise that the self (உள்ளம்) fills the whole body, so that both halves are alive, is the Jain view of the soul as coextensive with its body; the verse does not name the school, but it is the doctrine the argument needs. The dilemma leaves the receiver either a killer or the taker of a corpse.

claims.claim: the self is present throughout the body, so whoever takes a living half is the giver's killer
a body without awareness is a corpse, and to give a corpse is no gift

216.reading: Neelakesi calls it folly to hold that when the body is cut into pieces the life within goes off separately with each, and asks whether any clear-minded person would trust the 'ultimate truth' that comes from a vulture's mouth.
216.nuance: பரமார்த்தம் is the Buddhist term for ultimate truth; பாறு வாய் (vulture's mouth) mocks it as carrion talk. What the opponent is said to hold about the divided life is inferred from the gift tales, not quoted from a Buddhist text.

claims.claim: the life does not divide and go separately when the body is cut into parts

217.reading: Neelakesi points to the tale of the adorned woman who saw the Buddha's beauty and begged him to unite with her: if he would not grant her that grace, to say he split open his own head for a petitioner is a deceit.
217.nuance: The point is consistency: a compassion that gives the head to one asker but refuses another's desire is not the boundless giving Kundalakesi claimed. Which tale is meant cannot be fixed from the verse.

218.reading: If dying in vain, knowing that nothing will come of it, is the excellence of your Bodhisattvas, Neelakesi asks, would not the woman who burns on the pyre with the husband who guarded her also have high virtue?
218.nuance: A reductio: the wife's death on the pyre is offered as the absurd consequence the Buddhists would have to praise. The phrase ஆவது இன்மை அறிந்தும் (knowing nothing comes of it) is the Jain description; a Buddhist would not grant that the Bodhisattva's death achieved nothing.

claims.claim: to die in vain, knowing nothing will come of it, is the excellence of the Bodhisattvas

219.reading: Neelakesi takes the tale of the patient sage who, while preaching dharma as peace, was cut down by a wicked man with a fierce weapon and gave way to his attacker, and calls it the lie among lies.
219.nuance: காந்தி (patience, Sanskrit kshanti) and கலகன் seem to name the Kshantivadin tale and its king; the reading of lines 2 and 4 (கலகன்றான், இடம் போந்து கொண்டதும்) is uncertain.

claims.claim: the Bodhisattva's patience that yields to the one who strikes him is a mark of his greatness

220.reading: Neelakesi appears to ask why, if the gods are seen worshipping where the Tathagata took the form of an elephant, he did not become fish and other creatures when they too were in pain: is that the nature of the Tathagata?
220.nuance: Line 1 (யானை யுள்ளா செங்குள தங்கெலாம்) is probably corrupt; the reading of the whole verse as a charge of selective compassion rests on line 4's ததாகதர் தன்மையோ.

221.reading: Against the tale that, born a monkey, he took pity on his troop when hunters came to kill them and saved them, Neelakesi asks where there are monkeys that cannot leap straight across, since monkeys by nature leap from tree to tree.
221.nuance: The objection is to the tale's need, not its kindness: a bridge of the monkey-king's body was useless to creatures that leap.

222.reading: If it is said that those of good conduct stretch themselves far for others, Neelakesi asks whether it is greatness for a monkey to lie stretching out its tail, not seeing that hands and feet are for rising against those who come to kill.
222.nuance: சீலம் is the Buddhist term for moral conduct. The verse sets resistance or flight, what limbs are for, against the self-offering the tale praises.

claims.claim: those of good conduct stretch themselves out for others even to their own death

223.reading: If you say that giving the red blood of one's own body to a demon is a great gift, Neelakesi asks, would giving all human filth to dogs then be good dharma?
223.nuance: Line 1 (தாய்க்கொன்றான்) does not divide with confidence; the reductio in lines 3 and 4 is clear: a gift is not dharma merely because something of the body is handed to a creature that wants it.

claims.claim: giving one's blood to a demon is a great gift

224.reading: The king tells Kundalakesi that a one-sided teacher, saying 'this is what I will do', made up the fictions of the birth-tales, and bids her, doe-eyed one, give up her esteem for them.
224.nuance: ஏகாந்தன் (one who holds to a single side) carries the Jain charge against other schools of one-sidedness, set against their own many-sided view; கற்பங்கள் here reads as fabrications. The speaker is taken to be the king (கோன்) presiding over the debate, who in 174 promised to expel the loser; the verb சொன்னான் is masculine, so it is not Neelakesi.
224.event: The king gives his verdict to Kundalakesi that the Jataka tales are inventions and tells her to stop esteeming them.

claims.claim: the Jataka tales are fabrications of a one-sided teacher

225.reading: Those who keep the hare's tale under cover and tell it to outsiders as truth are fools, the verse says; the woman with tresses dark as rain-cloud spoke fittingly, and nothing she said ran against the words of the wise.
225.nuance: முயல் உரை is read as the hare tale (the Bodhisattva as a hare offering his body), the last of the Jataka gifts; முயல் could also mean effort. The verse changes metre, and the scribal forms எனெ and இருக்ந் in line 1 are corrupt. Whether lines 1 and 2 continue the king's verdict or are the narrator's is unclear.
225.event: The debate closes with Neelakesi judged to have spoken without contradiction.

226.reading: The king commands that the victory of the one whose words were dense with meaning be proclaimed quickly through the land, with the drum and the long banner sounding.
226.nuance: Lines 1 and 3 are corrupt in the edition (இட்ஜுசொலவவை நார்களு, முலூங்க); the gist, a drum proclamation ordered by the king, rests on lines 2 to 4.
226.event: The king orders Neelakesi's victory proclaimed with drum and banner.

227.reading: Kundalakesi is asked what remains now and who taught her this doctrine, and is told to say it quickly; she answers that it is the teacher Arkkachandran, who lives in the inner city on the south side of walled Ujjain.
227.nuance: Who asks is not stated: the address அன்னாய் and the plural நுமக்கு suit Neelakesi questioning the defeated debater. The text is corrupt in places (சும்க்கினை, எளூ, ம்க்கசந்திரன் for அர்க்கசந்திரன், அவாச்சியன் for ஆசாரியன்).
227.event: Kundalakesi, questioned, names Arkkachandran of Ujjain as her teacher.

228.reading: The townspeople, after many harsh words, beat the drum, shout many reproaches telling her not to come back, heap many insults on the fair-browed woman who had laughed as she entered the city after planting her rose-apple branch at the guarded gate, and drive her out of the city's gate.
228.nuance: This is the penalty the king announced before the debate (174): the loser is to be sent out with shame. The நாவல் branch is the challenge Kundalakesi planted at the gate (164, 169). A stray bracket before வாரலென்று in line 3 is an edition mark.
228.event: Kundalakesi is driven out of the city gate with drums and insults.

229.reading: The king, like a lion, thunder and a bull, says of Neelakesi, who is beautiful like a flowering creeper in a field, knows many books in their nature and is without fault: what is it fitting for me to do for her now?
229.event: The king asks what reward he should give Neelakesi.

230.reading: When the king said this, she of dharma, who wanted no jewels, gave no thought to adornment, and desired none of these, neither land nor great treasure, told the king: from now on, hold to the path of dharma here.
230.nuance: The reward is refused item by item (jewels, adornment, land, treasure) and replaced by a charge laid on the king; the winner's prize becomes his conduct. வேந்திழை in line 4 is ஏந்திழை with the glide of the preceding உறுக என.
230.event: Neelakesi refuses jewels, land and wealth and asks the king instead to follow the path of dharma.

claims.claim: a king should hold to the path of dharma

231.reading: Neelakesi tells the king that this is what she came for, and that with a lordship like Indra's he should not scorn the path of dharma; then, leaving him, she rises and sets out through the sky toward the quarter where Arkkachandran lives.
231.nuance: இந்திரன் அனைய repeats the comparison used of this king when Kundalakesi first arrived (166); the sky road is how Neelakesi travels between debates.
231.event: Neelakesi takes leave of the king and departs through the sky toward Arkkachandran.

claims.claim: a king's power, however great, must not scorn the path of dharma

links.note: The Kundalakesi's invocation praises its lord as one who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good (பிறர்க்கே உறுதிக்கு உழந்தான்); Neelakesi 222 mocks the monkey-king's self-offering, which saved no one, as no greatness.
links.teaches: The dispute is not whether the Buddha gave himself away but whether labour for others counts when, as the Jain argues, it profits no one; the Buddhist praise rests on intention, the Jain rebuttal on result.

links.note: Flesh eaten by birds: the Kundalakesi fragment shows vultures and dogs tearing the desired body; Neelakesi 214 says flesh cut off as a gift feeds only crows.
links.teaches: The same carrion image serves the Buddhist as a reason to stop desiring the body and the Jain as a reason not to throw it away, so contempt for the body and refusal to waste it come from one picture.

links.note: Kural 221 defines giving as giving to those who have nothing; Neelakesi 214 argues that a gift of flesh or an eye cannot become the receiver's and so fills no lack.
links.teaches: The Kural fixes a gift's worth by the receiver's want; the debate adds that the gift must also be usable by the receiver, which rules out the heroic gifts of the body.

gains.a: the Jain objection gains a recognised Tamil definition of giving to argue from
gains.b: the couplet's want-based test is extended to what is given, not only to whom

links.note: Kural 230 says death is sweet when one can no longer give; Neelakesi 218 says a death known to achieve nothing is no virtue, and draws the wife on the pyre as the absurd consequence.
links.teaches: The Kural's rank of giving above life is hyperbole about value; the Jain argument shows where taking it literally leads, and limits the praise of self-loss to a death that does something.

gains.a: the epic's limit on self-sacrifice is seen answering a Tamil maxim that ranks giving above living
gains.b: the couplet's hyperbole is shown needing a boundary once epics told of givers who literally died

links.note: Perunkoppendu argues for her place on her husband's pyre against the elders who hold her back; Neelakesi 218 cites the wife who burns with her guardian husband as the futile death no one should call virtue.
links.teaches: The Sangam queen gives the pyre a reason, escape from the widow's diet and gravel bed, that the Jain reductio ignores when it calls such death one that achieves nothing; the two disagree on what the wife's death is for.

gains.a: the epic's 'nothing comes of it' is tested against a widow who says exactly what comes of it
gains.b: the queen's choice is seen being cited later as the standard case of a death a moral argument rejects

links.note: Aathirai enters the pyre to go where her husband's deeds have carried him, but the fire will not touch her and a voice says he lives; Neelakesi 218 names the wife's death with her husband as the absurd end of praising futile death.
links.teaches: Neither epic lets a wife's death on the pyre stand as achieved virtue, the Jain by argument and the Buddhist by a fire that refuses her, yet the Manimekalai gives the karmic motive the Neelakesi's reductio leaves out.

links.note: Kundalakesi lists her lord's gifts of eyes, flesh, body, wife, land, child and heaven (205); the king's verdict in 224 calls those birth-tales fabrications of a one-sided teacher.
links.teaches: The debate is settled not by refuting each gift but by the king reclassifying the whole catalogue as fiction, so the Buddhist's chief proof of compassion is turned into the proof of one-sidedness.

links.note: Before the debate the king promised to send the loser out with shame (174); in 228 the townspeople drive Kundalakesi out of the gate with drums and insults.
links.teaches: The expulsion is the execution of a stake both debaters accepted with joy beforehand, so the shame is the contract of the debate rather than the mob's cruelty.

links.note: The defeated Kundalakesi names Arkkachandran of Ujjain as her teacher (227); 233 opens the next sarukkam on Arkkachandran in Ujjain.
links.teaches: Each defeat in the Neelakesi names the next opponent, so the chain of debates is built by the losers' own testimony of who taught them.

links.note: Given audience by the Chera, Nariveruuthalaiyar asks for nothing and tells him to guard the realm with grace and love; offered jewels, land and treasure, Neelakesi refuses them and tells the king to keep to the path of dharma.
links.teaches: The visitor who turns a king's favour into counsel persists from bardic to religious poetry, but the counsel shifts from ruling with grace to following a doctrine, and the refusal of gifts becomes a renouncer's mark.

gains.a: Neelakesi's scene is seen as a known Tamil form, the counsel given in place of a gift
gains.b: the Sangam form of counsel to a king is shown carried into a sectarian epic where the adviser wants nothing

new_concepts.gloss: the tales of the Buddha's former births as a Bodhisattva, told chiefly of his gifts of body, family and life
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word (neelakesi 212: சாதகம்; 224: சாதக கற்பங்கள்)

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools before a king and assembly, with stakes for the loser; distinct from vaadham, the alchemy of the Siddhars
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam title names it (குண்டலகேசி வாதச் சருக்கம்); the id is mine, since vaadham is taken

source_issues: 212: lines 1-2 (ஆதனாற் குறந்தாங்கெழுவான்றும்ம / வேதமில் சுடரேற்றொருதாமென்றான்) do not divide with confidence.
220: line 1 (யானை யுள்ளா செங்குள தங்கெலாம்) appears corrupt.
225: line 1 has scribal errors (எனெ, இருக்ந்); line 3 கோந்தலி for கூந்தலி. The verse changes metre from the preceding run.
226: lines 1 and 3 carry encoding damage (இட்ஜுசொலவவை, முலூங்க).
227: encoding damage (சும்க்கினை, எளூ, ம்க்கசந்திரன் for அர்க்கசந்திரன், அவாச்சியன்).
228: a stray '(' before வாரலென்று in line 3.
224: the speaker கோன் is read as the presiding king; the verse does not name him.
